title: Computing TCP's Retransmission Timer
summary: Defines the algorithm TCP senders must use to work out how long to wait for an acknowledgment before resending data. It expands on guidance in RFC 1122 and raises support for the algorithm from SHOULD to MUST. It replaced RFC 2988.

eli5.summary: When you send a letter and expect a reply, you decide how long to wait before writing again. This is the rule TCP follows to guess that waiting time, so it neither gives up too early nor waits too long.

questions: how does tcp compute retransmission timeout
how does tcp compute the retransmission timeout
what is the initial rto in tcp
subtitle: The standard recipe a TCP sender uses to decide how long to wait for an acknowledgment before resending.

tldr.problem: A TCP sender needs a retransmission timeout (RTO): too short and it resends data that was not lost, too long and it recovers slowly from real loss.
tldr.mechanism: The sender keeps a smoothed round-trip time and a variation estimate, sets the RTO to the smoothed value plus four times the variation, rounds up to at least 1 second, and doubles the RTO each time the timer expires.
tldr.outcome: Supporting the algorithm moves from SHOULD to MUST, the initial RTO drops from 3 seconds to 1 second, and the document obsoletes RFC 2988.

facts.label: Maximum RTO
facts.value: At least 60 seconds, if one is set

facts.label: Back off
facts.value: RTO doubles on each timer expiry

today: RFC 6298 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2988 and updates RFC 1122. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why TCP Needs a Timer Rule
sections.content:
TCP uses a retransmission timer to make sure data is delivered even when the receiver sends no feedback. The length of that timer is the RTO (retransmission timeout). RFC 1122 said the RTO should be calculated as in Van Jacobson's 1988 paper. RFC 6298 codifies that algorithm and raises the requirement to support it from a SHOULD to a MUST.

The RFC does not change how TCP behaves after the timer fires; that is covered by RFC 5681. It leaves room for caution: a sender may be more conservative than the algorithm allows, but it MUST NOT be more aggressive.
sections.eli5: TCP sends data and waits for a thank-you. This RFC says exactly how long to wait before sending again, and that you must never be too impatient.

sections.title: The Basic Algorithm
sections.content:
The sender keeps two state variables: SRTT, the smoothed round-trip time, and RTTVAR, the round-trip time variation. It also assumes a clock granularity of G seconds.

Before any round-trip measurement exists, the sender SHOULD set RTO to 1 second. When the first measurement R arrives, the sender MUST set SRTT = R, RTTVAR = R/2 and RTO = SRTT + max(G, K*RTTVAR), with K = 4.

For each later measurement R', the sender MUST update RTTVAR = (1 - beta) * RTTVAR + beta * |SRTT - R'| first, and then SRTT = (1 - alpha) * SRTT + alpha * R'. The order matters, since the RTTVAR update uses the old SRTT. It SHOULD use alpha = 1/8 and beta = 1/4. Then RTO is recomputed with the same formula.

Whenever RTO is computed and comes out under 1 second, it SHOULD be rounded up to 1 second. The RFC explains that a large minimum keeps TCP conservative, while acknowledging that future research might justify a smaller one. A maximum MAY be applied, provided it is at least 60 seconds.
sections.eli5: TCP keeps a running guess of how long a round trip takes and how much that time wobbles. It waits the average plus a safety cushion, and never less than a second.

sections.title: Taking Round-Trip Samples
sections.content:
TCP MUST use Karn's algorithm for taking samples: a sample MUST NOT be taken from a segment that was retransmitted, because it is unclear whether the acknowledgment answers the first copy or a later one. The one safe exception is when the TCP timestamp option is used, since it removes that ambiguity.

Implementations traditionally measured once per round trip. With timestamps, every acknowledgment can serve as a sample. A TCP MUST take at least one measurement per round trip, unless Karn's algorithm prevents it. The RFC notes that for modest congestion windows, timing every segment does not give a better estimator, and that adjusting alpha and beta when taking many samples per round trip is an open research question.
sections.eli5: If you shout the same question twice and hear one answer, you cannot tell which shout it replied to. So TCP does not time answers to repeated messages, unless each message carries a timestamp.

sections.title: Clock Granularity
sections.content:
The RFC puts no requirement on the clock granularity G. There is one rule: if the K*RTTVAR term would be zero, it MUST be rounded up to G seconds, which is what the max(G, K*RTTVAR) term does.

Experience showed that finer granularities, 100 msec or less, perform somewhat better than coarse ones. The RFC adds that Jacobson's paper describes tricks for getting better precision from coarse timers, and that these are widely implemented.
sections.eli5: A clock that only ticks once in a while cannot measure small gaps well. TCP works with such clocks, but a clock with finer ticks does a somewhat better job.

sections.title: Managing the Timer
sections.content:
An implementation MUST never retransmit a segment less than one RTO after its previous transmission. The RECOMMENDED timer management is a short list of rules.

  • When a data packet is sent and the timer is not running, start it for RTO seconds.
  • When all outstanding data is acknowledged, turn the timer off.
  • When an acknowledgment for new data arrives, restart the timer for RTO seconds.

When the timer expires, the sender retransmits the earliest unacknowledged segment, MUST set RTO = RTO * 2 (the back off), and restarts the timer with the new value. The maximum from the previous section may bound the doubling. If the timer expires while waiting for the ACK of a SYN and the implementation uses an RTO under 3 seconds, the RTO MUST be reset to 3 seconds when data transmission begins.

After a retransmission, the next new measurement runs the Section 2 computation again, which can collapse RTO back down. A TCP MAY clear SRTT and RTTVAR after backing off several times, since they are likely bogus by then, and re-initialize them from the next sample.
sections.eli5: If nobody answers, TCP waits, tries again, and then waits twice as long next time. When an answer finally arrives, it goes back to its normal waiting time.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
An attacker who adds delay to a timed packet or its acknowledgment can push the RTO up. The RFC points out that the ability to delay a packet usually comes with the ability to drop it, so it is hard to see what this gains beyond what simple discarding already offers.

An attacker could instead forge acknowledgments for segments the receiver has not received, lowering the RTO to an unsafe value and making the sender more aggressive. That requires spoofing acknowledgments correctly, which is difficult without seeing the path. Even then, the sender still backs off when a packet is truly lost to congestion. The security considerations of RFC 5681 also apply.
sections.eli5: A trickster could slow down or fake the replies to change how long TCP waits. The RFC says that is hard to do and rarely worth the trouble, since the trickster could just throw the messages away.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 2988
sections.content:
The main change is the initial RTO, lowered from 3 seconds to 1 second. If the SYN or the ACK of the SYN is lost, the RTO reverts to 3 seconds before data transmission begins.

Appendix A balances two goals: an initial RTO large enough to avoid spurious retransmissions, and small enough to recover quickly from loss before any sample exists. It cites studies where over 97.5% of observed connections had round-trip times under 1 second, and about 2.5% had longer ones, and retransmission rates of roughly 2% within the three-way handshake. For connections that fall back to 3 seconds, the cost is modest: an extra SYN and an initial congestion window limited to 1 segment. The authors conclude that the lower value is likely beneficial to many connections and harmful to relatively few.
sections.eli5: The old rule waited three seconds before the first retry. Since networks got faster, the new rule waits only one second, and goes back to three if that turns out to be too short.

data.title: Computing RTO
data.code:
First measurement R:
  SRTT   <- R
  RTTVAR <- R/2
  RTO    <- SRTT + max(G, K*RTTVAR)     (K = 4)

Later measurement R':
  RTTVAR <- (1 - beta) * RTTVAR + beta * |SRTT - R'|
  SRTT   <- (1 - alpha) * SRTT + alpha * R'
  RTO    <- SRTT + max(G, K*RTTVAR)

  alpha = 1/8, beta = 1/4

columns: After a lost SYN or SYN ACK
